A patient once asked me a question midway through a session that I should have welcomed more quickly.

“How do you know that’s the right place?”

I had a clinical explanation. I could describe the movement we were exploring, the symptoms they had reported, and why I had chosen that area. But the question wasn’t only about anatomy. It was also about whether the person on the table could understand what I was doing—and whether they were allowed to challenge it.

I answered the question. Then I noticed something about the encounter: until that moment, I had been treating my reasoning as though it were already shared.

Trust can be mistaken for a patient’s willingness to go along with us. They book the appointment, get on the table, and let us work. We may interpret that cooperation as confidence in our judgment. But agreeing to receive care is not the same as understanding every decision made during it.

In clinical practice, trust is less useful as a feeling we hope to inspire than as a relationship we have to keep making understandable.

Explain the decision, not just the technique

A patient does not need a lecture in anatomy to participate in care. They do need a way to understand what we are trying to accomplish.

When I explain why I want to examine a movement or work in a particular area, I give the patient something they can respond to. They can tell me whether the explanation fits their experience. They can correct an assumption. They can ask what happens if we choose another approach.

This is not a performance of expertise. It is an invitation to examine the plan together.

There are times when I am uncertain. Saying so does not erase the value of my experience. It distinguishes what I observed from what I suspect, and what we know from what we still need to learn.

Trust has room for that distinction.

Make your behavior predictable

The treatment room contains many small moments of uncertainty.

A patient may not know where my hands will move next, how much pressure I intend to use, how long a position will be held, or whether speaking up will interrupt the work. Those uncertainties may be minor to me and significant to them.

Predictability does not require narrating every movement. It means giving enough information that the next step is not an unwelcome surprise.

I can describe what I propose, check whether it is acceptable, and follow through on what we agreed. If I need to change the plan, I can say so before I change it.

Over time, consistency between what I say and what I do gives the patient a basis for deciding whether to rely on me. The point is not to appear perfectly certain. It is to be dependable when circumstances change.

Leave room for disagreement

One of the clearest tests of a therapeutic relationship is what happens when the patient says no.

Perhaps they do not want a particular area treated. Perhaps an approach that made sense to me does not feel right to them. Perhaps they want to stop, ask a question, or pursue a different goal.

If I treat that response as resistance to overcome, I have changed the terms of the relationship. The patient is now being asked to defend a boundary that should already belong to them.

I can explain my reasoning, including any meaningful tradeoffs. I can offer alternatives. I can also accept that the patient may choose differently than I would.

A person’s ability to disagree is not evidence that trust has failed. It may be evidence that the relationship allows honest participation.

Respond when trust is tested

Even careful clinicians miss things.

I may misunderstand a goal, use language that confuses, or move faster than a patient expected. A patient may tell me that something feels uncomfortable or that I have not heard what they were trying to say.

The important question then is not whether I can defend my intention. It is whether I can recognize the effect and respond.

I can stop, acknowledge what I missed, ask what would be helpful, and change my behavior. An explanation may be useful, but it should not replace listening.

A therapeutic alliance does not depend on never making a mistake. It depends, in part, on whether a mistake can be named and addressed without making the patient responsible for protecting the clinician’s confidence.

Let trust remain the patient’s decision

We sometimes speak of “building trust” as though it were a technique with a predictable result.

It isn’t.

A clinician can act transparently, communicate clearly, respect boundaries, and remain accountable. Those actions create reasons a patient might choose to trust us. They do not entitle us to that trust.

And trust is not unlimited. A patient may trust my skill in one area and want more explanation in another. They may trust me today and reconsider tomorrow. They may value our work and still decide that another clinician is better suited to the next step.

That freedom matters.

The Tao of clinical touch is not an argument for passive care. It asks us to notice how much of the encounter depends on what we do before, during, and after an intervention.

Skill gives us something to offer.

Trust asks whether the person receiving it can see our reasoning, question our choices, and remain fully present in the decisions that concern their own body.

The Clinical Practice of Restraint

There is a moment in almost every treatment when the clinician has a choice.

The technique is working—or at least something is happening. The patient has given us information. We could continue, increase the pressure, move to the next structure, or introduce another approach. We could also stop long enough to ask whether the next intervention has earned its place.

Experience does not eliminate that decision. It makes us more accountable for it.

We accumulate techniques because we want to help. Over time, a larger repertoire can make it easier to find something to do and harder to notice when doing something else is unnecessary. A treatment plan can quietly become a sequence we feel obliged to finish. But the person on the table did not come to experience the full range of our skills. They came with a concern, a goal, and a nervous system responding to the encounter in real time.

Clinical restraint begins there. Not with the instruction to do less, but with the discipline to make each intervention answer to a purpose.

The intervention needs a reason

Before I choose a technique, I need to know what I am asking it to accomplish.

That purpose might be to explore a movement that has become uncomfortable, make a familiar activity easier, or help someone tolerate touch in an area that has felt threatening. The purpose should make sense to the patient as well as to me. It should also leave room for the possibility that my first idea is wrong.

Without a reason, the treatment risks becoming a tour of findings. One restricted area leads to another. Every new observation becomes an invitation to intervene. The session fills with activity, but the relationship between that activity and the patient’s priorities grows less clear.

A clear indication does not guarantee a result. It gives us something more valuable: a reason to begin and a basis for deciding whether to continue.

The dose is a clinical decision

Once an intervention has a purpose, we still have to choose its dose.

In hands-on care, dose is not only pressure. It includes pace, duration, repetition, the number of areas addressed, the complexity of the encounter, and the amount of new information we ask someone to process. These variables are not badges of effort. They are clinical decisions.

A patient may welcome firm contact and respond well to it. Another may prefer a lighter approach, or need time to establish what feels tolerable. Neither response makes one style universally correct. The question is whether the input is appropriate for this person, in this moment, in service of the agreed goal.

When I match the intervention to the response rather than asking the response to justify my preferred intervention, restraint becomes a form of precision.

That does not mean avoiding challenge. Sometimes the work calls for a carefully negotiated challenge. The distinction is whether we are testing a useful possibility together or simply adding intensity because we can.

Reassess before you add more

The next decision is often the most easily skipped.

Something feels different under my hands. The patient reports a change. Perhaps movement is easier; perhaps it is not. The temptation is to interpret any change as permission to continue—or to add something else in pursuit of a more impressive result.

But a change is information, not an instruction.

Reassessment brings us back to the original purpose. What does the patient notice? Has the movement or activity we agreed to explore changed in a meaningful way? Has the intervention introduced discomfort, fatigue, uncertainty, or an unexpected response? Does the next step still have a reason?

Not every response can be explained in the moment, and not every useful observation proves a particular physiological mechanism. We can be attentive without pretending certainty.

A plan that cannot change in response to new information is no longer a clinical plan. It is a performance.

Change the plan, not the patient

There is a subtle pressure that can enter a treatment when the clinician becomes invested in an approach.

We explain why it should work. We ask for a little more time. We encourage the patient to tolerate a little more intensity. Sometimes those choices are appropriate and mutually agreed upon. Sometimes they are signs that we are defending the plan instead of listening to the person.

Restraint asks us to notice the difference.

If the intervention is not serving its purpose, changing course is not a failure of confidence. It may be the clearest expression of it. We can adjust the input, reconsider the goal, ask a better question, or acknowledge that the next useful step lies beyond what this session—or our scope of practice—can provide.

Clinical authority is not the power to make every intervention work. It is the responsibility to make decisions that remain accountable to the person receiving care.

Know when the work is complete

A session has a scheduled ending. Useful intervention may have an earlier one.

Perhaps the agreed movement is easier and further work offers no clear advantage. Perhaps the patient has reached the amount of input they want today. Perhaps the response suggests that another approach, more time, or a referral would be more appropriate. In each case, the decision to stop deserves as much thought as the decision to begin.

This is not an argument for shorter sessions, lighter treatment, or doing the minimum. It is an argument against mistaking more intervention for more care.

Completion also changes how we close. We can describe what we observed, acknowledge uncertainty where it exists, and help the patient understand what to pay attention to without turning every sensation into a problem to monitor. We do not need to claim that we fixed them. We need to leave them with a clear understanding of what we did, why we stopped, and what choices remain available.

The Tao often points toward action without imposition. In clinical practice, that is not a mystical instruction to stand aside. It is the difficult, ordinary work of remaining responsive when our training, our habits, and even our desire to help urge us to do more.

Knowing a hundred techniques may expand our options.

Knowing why to choose one, when to change it, and when to put our hands down is what makes those options useful.

Words can protect regulation or reintroduce threat.

We spend years learning what to do with our hands.

How to assess.
How to palpate.
How to choose an intervention.
How to recognize when something changes.

We spend considerably less time learning what to say about what we find.

And yet the moment we give an experience a name, offer an explanation, or tell someone what we think is happening, we have introduced another clinical input.

Language.

The treatment does not end when our hands leave the body.

Sometimes, what we say next matters just as much.

What You Say Becomes Part of the Treatment

A client sits up after the session and asks the familiar question:

What did you find?

It is tempting to answer with certainty.

“Your hip is out.”

“This muscle is completely locked up.”

“You have a lot of scar tissue.”

“Your posture is causing this.”

These explanations can sound clinical. They can also become stories the client carries home.

A sensation that was simply uncomfortable now has a cause.

A movement that felt uncertain now has something supposedly wrong with it.

A body that hurt now has a problem to monitor.

Our words have changed the context in which the next sensation will be experienced.

That deserves our attention.

Expectation Changes Experience

Expectation is not imaginary.

What someone anticipates can influence how they attend to an experience, interpret it, and respond to it.

Tell someone, “This is probably going to hurt,” and you have given their nervous system information before the stimulus even arrives.

Tell them, “You may notice some sensation here. Let me know what you experience,” and you have done something different.

You have left room for discovery.

The difference may appear subtle.

Clinically, it is enormous.

One statement predicts an experience.

The other permits one.

This doesn’t mean withholding information or pretending everything will feel good. It means recognizing that our language participates in expectation.

And expectation enters the room before our hands do.

Do Not Give Pain a Story It Didn’t Ask For

People experiencing pain naturally want explanations.

We naturally want to provide them.

The danger begins when explanation becomes certainty.

We feel tension and call it dysfunction.

We notice asymmetry and call it imbalance.

We find tenderness and construct a mechanical story around it.

Perhaps that story is correct.

Perhaps it isn’t.

But once spoken with authority, it can become difficult for the client to separate what they actually experience from what we told them their experience means.

Clinical reasoning should help us investigate possibilities, not require the client to inherit our conclusions.

There is nothing clinically incomplete about acknowledging what we don’t yet know. Uncertainty can remain part of the assessment without becoming something we need to resolve for the client before we have enough information.

Recommend Without Creating Dependence

The same discipline matters when we discuss what comes next.

“You need to come back every week.”

“You’ll tighten right back up if we don’t stay on this.”

“This is something we’ll have to keep fixing.”

Listen to the relationship those sentences create.

The clinician becomes necessary.

The body becomes unreliable.

Care becomes something delivered to the client rather than something developed with them.

There may absolutely be reasons to recommend another session.

Explain what you observed. Describe what you would like to reassess. Offer a reasonable path forward.

But recommendation and dependence are not the same thing.

Good clinical communication helps people understand their options without convincing them that progress depends upon continued access to us.

Give Them Language They Can Leave With

Eventually, the client walks out the door.

What travels with them?

Perhaps soreness.

Perhaps relief.

Perhaps greater movement.

But also language.

The language we used to describe their body.

The language we used to explain their pain.

The language we used to frame what changed.

That language may influence what they notice tomorrow.

So give them words that preserve possibility.

“You moved differently afterward.”

“Let’s see how that feels over the next couple of days.”

“You don’t need to protect it just because you noticed it.”

“If something changes, that’s information. We can learn from it.”

We cannot control what happens after a treatment.

Nor should we try.

Our job is not to provide a story so convincing that the client cannot imagine another one.

It is to help create conditions in which they can continue discovering what their body is capable of.

Our hands may begin that conversation.

Our language helps determine whether it remains open.

The session is not the finish line.

That can be easy to forget.

A client gets off the table and says, “That feels different.” They move the shoulder that was bothering them. Turn their head. Take a deeper breath. Maybe they reach toward the floor and discover something that wasn’t available an hour ago.

We see it.

They feel it.

Something changed here.

And there is value in recognizing that moment.

But a change observed is not yet a change integrated.

Because then something important happens.

THEN THEY LEAVE.

The drive home.
The desk tomorrow.
The stairs.
The workout.

Life adds variables the treatment room cannot.

The session can create an experience. Life reveals what becomes available from it.

That distinction matters.

Our work does not exist so that someone can move beautifully for thirty seconds beside the treatment table. The session creates an opening. What happens with that opening belongs to everything that comes afterward.

Our role is to help create the conditions for that possibility.

The Session Is Not the Finish Line

There was a time in my career when the immediate change carried enormous weight.

Did the range of motion improve?

Did the pain decrease?

Did the tissue feel different?

Could the client do the thing they couldn’t do when they walked through the door?

Those observations still matter. They give us information. They can tell us that something meaningful occurred during the encounter.

But they don’t tell us the whole story.

The more interesting question often comes later.

What happens when nobody is watching?

Can they turn to back out of the driveway without thinking about their neck?

Can they reach into the back seat?

Can they get out of bed tomorrow morning and simply move?

Can they return to the gym, the garden, the office, the instrument, the child they pick up from the floor?

That’s where the treatment begins meeting the person’s actual life.

A change observed is real.

But the session is not the finish line.

It may only be the first place the person experiences what is now possible.

New Doesn’t Have to Mean Normal Yet

What becomes possible in the room still has to become recognizable outside it.

That takes time.

A newly available movement may still feel unfamiliar.

IT’S NEW. SO OF COURSE IT FEELS DIFFERENT.

We sometimes interpret unfamiliarity as evidence that something isn’t working. Clients can do this too.

But possibility may happen in a moment.

Familiarity takes time.

The nervous system has history. It has expectations. It has learned patterns of movement, protection, effort and attention. One different experience does not immediately erase all of that.

Nor does it need to.

Change can be available before it feels familiar.

That is an important distinction.

The nervous system remembers—not in a moment, but through repetition.

So perhaps the question after treatment isn’t simply, Does it still feel better?

Maybe it is:

What are you noticing now?

That question leaves room for discovery.

It doesn’t demand that the client reproduce what happened on the table. It doesn’t turn the treatment into a test they can pass or fail.

It allows something new to remain new for a while.

Pause Creates Perspective

And familiarity alone isn’t integration.

Sometimes the person needs enough distance from the session to recognize what actually changed.

Experience becomes more useful when there is space to understand what it means.

That may happen tomorrow.

Or three days from now.

A client may not notice the change while deliberately checking for it. They may notice it when they reach for something without hesitation, sleep differently, turn their head while driving, or finish an activity and realize afterward that the familiar limitation never entered their awareness.

A moment of reflection can turn experience into understanding.

When we pause, we create space to see more clearly—not just what is happening, but what it means.

That is why reflection matters.

It helps us recognize patterns, connections and new possibilities that are difficult to see while we’re still standing inside the experience.

And this applies to us as clinicians too.

We don’t always need to rush toward the next intervention, explanation or conclusion.

Sometimes better questions emerge in the space between the doing.

What changed?

What remained?

What became easier?

What became possible?

What did the person discover that neither of us predicted?

The pause is not stepping away from the work.

Sometimes the pause is what allows us to understand the work.

Change Has to Find a Life Outside the Room

Eventually, noticing matters less than using.

What happens in treatment matters.

What becomes usable afterward matters more.

This is where clinical success can become deceptively difficult to recognize.

Because when integration really begins, the treatment itself can start disappearing from the story.

The person isn’t thinking about the technique.

They aren’t thinking about the muscle.

They aren’t thinking about the conversation we had or the clever thing we thought we discovered.

They are simply doing something.

Everyday movement gives treatment its context.

It’s where change becomes useful.

When she can use it without thinking about the treatment, integration has begun.

That is a very different measure of success from needing the client to remember exactly what we did.

The work doesn’t need to stay connected to us.

It needs to become connected to her life.

And that changes the role of the clinician.

We can observe.

We can listen.

We can create conditions.

We can offer another experience of movement, touch, safety or possibility.

But ultimately, whatever becomes available has to survive outside the environment we created for it.

Integration isn’t the end of the work.

It’s where the work starts to live.

The Change Was Never Ours to Keep

And this may be the most important transition of all.

There comes a point when the change should no longer belong to the treatment.

The clinician can help create possibility.

The life that possibility enters belongs to the person.

That can challenge us.

We spend years learning how to become more effective. We study. We practice. We refine our touch. We learn anatomy, movement, pain science, communication and technique.

Naturally, we want the work to matter.

But perhaps one of the clearest signs that it mattered is that eventually we matter less.

The clinical encounter can open a possibility.

But the next movement, the next choice, the next experience happens in their world.

What became possible in the room can become ordinary somewhere else.

No reminder of the treatment.

No need to prove the change.

Just life being lived.

There is something deeply respectful about that.

It removes the clinician from the center of the story.

We were there.

We participated.

Perhaps we helped create the conditions in which something different could happen.

But we don’t own what happened next.

And we shouldn’t need to.

Continuity isn’t keeping the treatment alive. It’s allowing what became possible to become part of a life.

The possibility may begin with us.

The life it enters belongs to them.

Range improves.

Guarding decreases.

Movement becomes easier.

We feel the change beneath our hands. We see it when we reassess. We compare where someone started with where they finished, and because it happened while we were working with them, it is easy to believe the change belongs to us.

It does not.

We may have participated in it. Our hands, reasoning, communication, pacing, pressure, timing, and restraint may have helped create the conditions in which change became possible.

But the person still has to decide whether that change is safe enough to keep.

Agency begins there.

The Change Is Not Yours

Practitioner participation is not the same as ownership.

We can guide movement. We can alter the environment. We can offer information, support, reassurance, challenge, and possibility.

But we cannot make another nervous system trust the result.

At some point, the person has to experience the change as something available to them rather than something produced by us.

That distinction does not diminish clinical work. It makes the work more precise.

You can create the conditions. The body still has to choose.

Better on the Table Is Not the Finish Line

The shoulder moves farther.

Pain decreases.

Tone softens.

The before-and-after comparison looks convincing. Something changed.

But what happens when your hands are no longer guiding the movement?

A person may comfortably allow a movement passively and still hesitate when asked to initiate it themselves. That does not make the improvement false. It tells us there is another question to ask:

What does this person trust themselves to do?

Because the movement that matters is not confined to a treatment table.

It is reaching into the cabinet tomorrow morning. Putting on a shirt. Lifting a child. Returning to training. Moving without first checking whether it is going to hurt.

Change observed is not always change owned.

Let Them Try

There comes a point when we need to remove our hands.

Then ask:

Try that again.

Now we are learning something different.

Does the person initiate easily?

Do they hesitate?

Brace?

Hold their breath?

Does the movement that appeared under our guidance remain available when they are responsible for producing it?

We are not simply testing whether the treatment worked. We are giving the person an opportunity to experience the movement as their own.

If the movement becomes smaller, that is not failure. If uncertainty returns, that is not failure either.

It is information.

Agency cannot be demonstrated by the practitioner.

At some point, your hands have to leave.

Know When to Step Back

Clinical skill is often measured by what we know how to do.

There is another skill that matters just as much:

Knowing when to stop doing it.

Move here. Relax this. Try again. Let me help.

Each may be useful at the right moment. But if every successful movement continues to require our hands, our reassurance, or our instruction, where does the confidence live?

Still with us.

There comes a point when guidance has done its job.

Remove the hands. Allow exploration. Let hesitation occur without immediately correcting it. Watch what the person discovers.

Stepping back is not abandonment. And doing less is not automatically better.

The question is whether our continued involvement is still helping someone discover their capacity or beginning to replace their experience of it.

Guidance creates possibility. Space allows ownership.

They Have to Own the Change

Years ago, I worked with a patient whose shoulder had become increasingly restricted.

We made progress. Range improved. Pain decreased. Movement became easier.

Then I went away on vacation.

While I was gone, she left me a voicemail.

She had clasped her bra behind her back for the first time in years.

But that was not the part that stayed with me.

She had not prepared for the movement. She had not tested the shoulder first. She had not waited for me to tell her it was safe.

She simply moved.

At the time, I thought the breakthrough had happened during treatment.

I understand it differently now.

The important moment happened when I was not there.

Her nervous system no longer needed my hands to demonstrate the possibility. She trusted the movement enough to initiate it herself.

That is agency.

Our work takes place in relationship. But the relationship is not meant to make the practitioner indispensable.

Sometimes the best evidence of our work happens when we are not there to see it.

Agency is what remains when the practitioner steps away.

We like plans.

They give shape to uncertainty.

A person arrives. We listen to what brought them in. We observe. We assess. We form a hypothesis about what might be useful.

Then we begin.

That process matters.

But there’s a problem if we think clinical reasoning ends there.

Because the moment we begin doing something, we create new information.

The person responds.

And suddenly the person in front of us may not be exactly the same person we assessed at the beginning of the session.

The Plan Is Only the Beginning

I don’t think good clinical practice requires us to arrive without a plan.

Quite the opposite.

Preparation matters.

A hypothesis matters.

Experience matters.

The mistake is treating any of those things as a contract with the future.

A plan is built from the information available when we make it.

Then the encounter begins.

Pressure is applied.

Movement is explored.

A position changes.

A question is asked.

Something feels easier.

Something becomes uncomfortable.

The person becomes more confident.

Or less certain.

Their breathing changes.

Their language changes.

Their expectation changes.

Every one of those things can become new information.

The question isn’t whether our original plan was good.

The question is whether we’re willing to let new information influence it.

What Changed?

There’s a question I think deserves a more regular place in clinical practice:

What changed?

Not:

Did my technique work?

Not:

Was my assessment correct?

Not even:

Is their range of motion better?

Just:

What changed?

That question is deliberately wider.

Maybe movement changed.

Maybe discomfort changed.

Maybe confidence changed.

Maybe the person understands the sensation differently.

Maybe nothing measurable changed, but they’re less apprehensive about moving.

Maybe the pressure that initially felt useful now feels excessive.

Maybe something we expected to change didn’t.

All of that is information.

And it creates an interesting clinical responsibility.

We have to decide whether what we just learned should change what we do next.

Not Every Response Requires More

This is where another habit can appear.

When something isn’t changing, we do more.

More pressure.

More technique.

More time.

More explanation.

More specificity.

I understand the impulse.

Doing something feels active.

And when someone has trusted us with their time, body, and money, activity can easily become confused with value.

But responsiveness isn’t measured by how much we do.

Sometimes new information suggests that we should add something.

Sometimes it suggests we should change direction.

Sometimes it suggests we should reduce what we’re doing.

And sometimes the most useful response is to stop interfering long enough to find out what happens next.

That requires a kind of restraint that isn’t always celebrated in hands-on care.

Knowing how to do something is a skill.

Knowing when not to do it is also a skill.

Don’t Turn Every Signal Into a Story

There’s another side to responsiveness.

We can respond too quickly.

A person moves differently after an intervention and our minds immediately begin constructing an explanation.

We changed the tissue.

We reduced guarding.

We improved mobility.

We found the problem.

Maybe.

Or maybe the movement was simply different the second time.

Maybe the person understood the instruction differently.

Maybe they felt safer.

Maybe they tried harder.

Maybe the change is real and meaningful but our explanation for it isn’t.

Observation and interpretation are not the same thing.

That’s why I think the magnitude of our response should match the strength of the information.

A small change may justify a small adjustment.

A repeated pattern may give us greater confidence.

Several pieces of information pointing in the same direction may justify changing the plan more substantially.

But one observation doesn’t have to become an entire story.

Respond to what you know. Not everything you can imagine.

A Response Can Be a Question

One of the easiest things to forget in clinical reasoning is that we aren’t the only source of information in the room.

Something changes.

Before deciding what it means, we can ask.

What did you notice?

Does that feel different?

Different how?

Is that useful?

Would you like to continue?

Those aren’t pauses in the treatment.

They are part of the treatment.

A question allows another nervous system, another history, and another perspective to enter the reasoning process.

It also gives us something we could never generate entirely through observation:

the person’s experience of what just happened.

We don’t have to convert every piece of information into another technique.

Sometimes the appropriate clinical response is curiosity.

Response Completes the Loop

For the past several weeks, I’ve been exploring a progression:

Understanding → Preparation → Permission → Listening → Timing → Possibility → Response

At first glance, that looks like a sequence.

I’m beginning to think it’s a loop.

Understanding helps us prepare.

Preparation creates room for permission.

Permission allows us to listen.

Listening changes our timing.

Timing opens possibility.

Possibility gives us more than one way to respond.

And our response creates new information.

So we listen again.

Maybe that’s a more useful way to think about clinical reasoning.

Not as the process that helps us discover the correct intervention.

But as the process that keeps us responsive while the encounter changes.

We don’t have to make the right decision once.

We have to remain available to the information that tells us what the next decision should be.

Response begins when new information is allowed to matter.

Last week, I didn’t publish a blog.

That wasn’t an oversight.

I was in Denver for the AMTA National Convention, and I made a conscious decision that my time was better spent preparing, presenting, listening, and being present with the people around me.

Coming home, I’m glad I did.

Because I don’t think I could have written this week’s piece before I went.

I arrived in Denver with nearly 30 years of clinical experience. I’ve spent decades with my hands on people. I’ve taught. I’ve presented. I’ve written a book. I’ve stood in front of rooms before.

I had every reason to feel confident.

And I did.

But confidence wasn’t the only thing that came with me.

My nervous system came too.

Knowing and Guarding Can Exist Together

There was a strange contradiction happening inside me.

I knew I belonged there.

At the same time, some part of me was still watching.

Guarding.

Waiting for the negative response.

Waiting for someone to challenge whether I belonged at the front of the room. Waiting to discover that perhaps other people didn’t see me the way I had begun to see myself.

And then something very different happened.

People came up to meet me.

Some told me they had been following my work. Some wanted to talk about The Tao of Clinical Touch. Some wanted a book signed.

And I found myself working alongside younger, passionate educators who brought their own ideas, experience, questions, and energy into the room.

A few referred to me as a mentor.

Others told me they were honored to meet me.

I’ll admit it.

That felt strange.

But it also made me proud.

Not proud because I had somehow arrived at the place where I had all the answers.

Almost the opposite.

I was beginning to recognize how much I have to contribute and how much I still have to learn.

More than one thing can be true.

Sometimes We Need to Zoom Out

I’ve spent much of this year writing and talking about what happens when the nervous system doesn’t immediately interpret an experience as safe.

We guard.

We predict.

We prepare.

We use previous experience to anticipate what might happen next.

Those responses make sense clinically.

Apparently, they make sense standing in front of a classroom in Denver too.

What surprised me was realizing that some of the very ideas I have been asking clinicians to consider were helping me understand my own experience.

Instead of judging the nervousness, I could notice it.

Instead of treating it as evidence that I didn’t belong, I could zoom out.

Thirty years of experience didn’t disappear because part of me was nervous.

Confidence and vulnerability could exist at the same time.

So could teacher and student.

So could mentor and colleague.

More than one thing can be true.

And when I stopped requiring one of those truths to defeat the others, something opened.

Leave Room for What You Didn’t Expect

I went to Denver prepared to teach.

I expected to help.

I expected conversations with colleagues and therapists.

I expected to talk about the book.

I even brought an invention I’ve been quietly developing because I thought the convention might be an opportunity to begin showing it to people.

I had a plan.

What I couldn’t plan was how the experience would feel.

I couldn’t plan someone telling me I had influenced the way they practice.

I couldn’t plan younger educators treating my experience as something valuable while simultaneously reminding me how much their curiosity and enthusiasm could teach me.

I couldn’t plan the feeling of realizing that perhaps my role in this profession is changing.

That doesn’t mean leaving clinical practice behind.

It means recognizing that experience creates another responsibility:

to share it.

And sharing doesn’t mean standing at the front of the room delivering answers.

Sometimes it means entering a room with everything you’ve learned and remaining open enough to discover what everyone else brought with them.

A plan should organize the encounter.

It shouldn’t seal it.

The Outcome May Not Look Like the Plan

That’s true in treatment.

It turns out it’s true in life as well.

We often decide what success should look like before an experience begins.

Then we measure ourselves against that prediction.

But some of the most meaningful outcomes in Denver weren’t things I would have thought to measure.

A conversation in the hallway.

Watching someone else’s teaching style.

A therapist holding my book.

A younger educator calling me a mentor.

The realization that being respected doesn’t require pretending I have nothing left to learn.

None of those were on my schedule.

They may have been among the most important things that happened.

Possibility Is the Practice

Over the past several weeks, I’ve been exploring a progression:

Understanding → Preparation → Permission → Listening → Timing → Possibility

I originally thought about that sequence through the lens of clinical encounters.

Denver reminded me that these aren’t principles we apply only to the people on our tables.

We live inside them too.

Possibility isn’t optimism.

It isn’t believing everything will work out.

And it certainly isn’t the absence of nervousness or uncertainty.

Possibility is what appears when we stop demanding that an experience confirm the story we carried into it.

I arrived in Denver with 30 years of experience.

I came home with 30 years of experience and more questions.

More people I want to learn from.

More people I want to teach.

More confidence in what I have to offer.

And perhaps a little more willingness to allow myself to feel proud when someone tells me it mattered.

I didn’t expect all of that.

Fortunately, I left enough room for it to happen.

Possibility is what becomes available when we stop needing to be right.

Issue 008: The Plan Must Be Allowed to Change

There is a quiet pressure in clinical work to be right early.

A client describes what is happening. We ask questions. We observe movement. We palpate. We begin connecting information. Before long, an explanation starts to form.

That is useful. Clinical work needs direction.

The problem begins when direction quietly becomes obligation.

Once we have explained what we think is happening, chosen a treatment strategy, and begun working, it can become surprisingly difficult to let the encounter change our mind.

Not because we are careless.

Often because we are trying to be competent.

We want our reasoning to hold together. We want the plan to make sense. We want the session to feel coherent.

But coherence is not the same as accuracy.

The first plan is built from incomplete information

Every treatment begins with a limitation that cannot be removed: we do not yet know everything that will happen during the encounter.

We know what the person has told us. We know what we observed before treatment. We know what our assessment suggested. We know what our experience tells us is plausible.

That is enough to form a working hypothesis.

It is not enough to stop listening.

Once treatment begins, the person continues to provide information.

A movement changes after an intervention. A symptom becomes clearer. A sensation appears in a position that seemed comfortable moments earlier. Pressure that was initially welcome becomes too much. A technique produces a response that does not match what we expected.

None of that information is an interruption to the plan.

It is part of the plan.

Clinical reasoning continues after the decision

We sometimes talk about clinical reasoning as though it happens before treatment.

Assess. Decide. Treat.

But experienced clinical work is rarely that linear.

A more useful description may be:

Observe. Form a hypothesis. Act carefully. Observe again. Compare the response with what you expected. Reconsider what you think you know.

Then continue.

The reasoning does not end when the first technique begins.

It becomes more informed.

That distinction changes the meaning of revision.

If the purpose of the session is to prove the original hypothesis, changing course can feel like failure.

If the purpose is to understand and help the person in front of us, changing course can be evidence that attention is still active.

The person is not required to confirm our explanation

Clinical experience gives us patterns.

Patterns are useful because they help us recognize possibilities quickly. They can make assessment more efficient and help us choose reasonable starting points.

But a pattern is not the person.

The moment we become more interested in preserving the pattern than understanding the response, the hierarchy changes.

Now the person is being asked to fit the explanation.

That is where a useful hypothesis can become a constraint.

The better question is not, “How do I make this treatment work?”

It may be, “What is this response asking me to reconsider?”

Sometimes the answer is very little.

Change the pressure. Adjust the position. Slow the pace. Ask another question.

Sometimes the answer is larger.

Change the technique. Change the goal. Reconsider the assumption that organized the session in the first place.

The size of the revision matters less than our willingness to notice when revision is needed.

Precision can include changing your mind

We often associate precision with consistency.

Do the right thing accurately and repeatably.

There is value in that. Skill matters. Technique matters. Knowledge matters.

But clinical precision also depends on responsiveness.

The right intervention at the beginning of an encounter may not remain the right intervention twenty minutes later.

The person has changed because the encounter has changed.

New information exists now that did not exist when the plan was formed.

Precision means allowing that information to matter.

This does not require abandoning structure or chasing every new sensation. It requires something quieter.

Availability.

The willingness to remain close enough to the encounter that the next piece of information can still influence what happens next.

A working hypothesis should remain workable

There is a reason I like the language of a working hypothesis.

It gives us permission to be thoughtful without pretending to be certain.

It allows us to bring our training, experience, and clinical judgment into the room while leaving space for the person to teach us something we did not know at the beginning.

That is not indecision.

It is disciplined curiosity.

We begin somewhere.

We pay attention.

We let the response become information.

And when the information changes, we remain willing to change with it.

Perhaps one of the clearest signs of clinical reasoning is not how confidently we can explain the first plan.

It is how thoughtfully we can recognize when the person in front of us is asking for a better one.

Reflection

Think about a recent session that did not unfold the way you expected.

When did you first notice the plan needed to change?

And what helped you trust that changing course was not leaving the reasoning behind, but continuing it?

In Issue 007, we explored how permission can change before it is spoken. This week, we look at what happens when the clinical plan itself must be allowed to change.

title.rendered: The Answer May Change Before It Is Spoken

content.rendered:
A client says yes to treatment.

The position feels fine. The pressure feels appropriate. The plan makes sense.

Then something changes.

The breath shortens. A hand that had been resting softly begins to grip the sheet. The shoulder you are working near becomes less available. Conversation that had been easy becomes quiet.

Nothing has been said.

That does not mean you know what the change means.

It does mean there may be something worth noticing.

Permission has a timeline

Monday’s idea was simple: permission is not a question.

A yes can begin an encounter. It cannot speak for everything that follows.

Tuesday took the next step: the body can change its answer. Pressure can feel different after several minutes. A position can become uncomfortable. A sensation can shift. An expectation can change once the experience becomes real.

Wednesday asks what happens before the person puts that change into words.

Clinical care does not require us to interpret every movement, breath, or expression. It does require us to remain available to the possibility that the experience has changed.

That distinction matters.

A change is information, not a conclusion

A deeper breath does not automatically mean relaxation.

A shorter breath does not automatically mean discomfort.

A hand movement does not automatically mean stop.

Silence does not automatically mean withdrawal.

People move. They adjust. They think. They remember something. They become distracted. They become comfortable. They become less comfortable.

The mistake is not failing to decode every cue correctly.

The mistake is deciding that a cue means something before the person has had a chance to tell you.

Observation can open a conversation. It should not replace one.

Notice the change from baseline

One of the most useful things a clinician can notice is not a single posture or behavior, but a shift.

What was happening a moment ago?

What is happening now?

Did the breathing pattern change when the pressure changed?

Did guarding appear after the position was adjusted?

Did the conversation become quieter when the treatment moved into a more sensitive area?

Did the client begin repositioning after several minutes in one posture?

None of those observations gives you the answer.

They may tell you it is time to make room for one.

The check-in does not need to be dramatic

You do not have to stop the entire session and announce that you noticed something.

Sometimes a simple question is enough.

“How is this feeling now?”

“Anything you would like different?”

“Still okay here?”

“Would another position feel better?”

The purpose is not to make the client defend the original yes.

It is to make changing the answer easy.

That is a different kind of permission.

It says the encounter is allowed to evolve.

Ongoing permission is not constant interrogation

There is another extreme worth avoiding.

If every breath, twitch, movement, or silence produces a question, the client may feel watched rather than cared for.

Permission-based practice is not surveillance.

It is responsiveness.

The clinician stays attentive enough to notice meaningful changes and restrained enough not to turn those changes into a story too quickly.

Sometimes the right response is to continue.

Sometimes it is to adjust.

Sometimes it is to ask.

Sometimes it is simply to wait long enough for the person to speak.

The clinical skill is availability

The initial conversation still matters.

Clear expectations still matter.

Good assessment still matters.

Technique still matters.

But none of those eliminates the need to remain available to new information once treatment begins.

A client should not have to overcome the momentum of your plan in order to change course.

If the body, the conversation, or the experience shifts, the encounter should still have room to shift with it.

That does not mean every change requires stopping.

It means every person should remain free to update the answer.

Reflection

Think about your last few sessions.

Was there a moment when something changed before the client said anything?

What did you notice?

What did you assume?

And did your practice make it easy for the person to give you a different answer?

That may be where ongoing permission becomes visible.

Every treatment begins before contact.

Before assessment. Before palpation. Before technique.

Long before our hands arrive, another conversation is already unfolding.

It begins with preparation.

Not simply whether the table is made or the room is clean. Preparation includes the conditions we create before another person enters our care: the environment, our attention, our pace, and our presence.

None of these replace clinical skill.

They shape the conditions in which clinical skill can be received.

A client does not arrive as a collection of tissues waiting to be assessed. They arrive already experiencing the room, the interaction, and us. They are noticing what feels predictable and what does not. They are gathering information before we have asked the first question.

So are we.

That makes the moments before touch clinically meaningful.

There is work in preparing the room so it feels intentional rather than hurried. There is work in arriving ourselves before asking someone else to settle. There is work in resisting the urge to move immediately toward explanation, assessment, or intervention simply because those are the parts of care we have been trained to recognize as productive.

Sometimes preparation is quieter than that.

It may be the pace of the greeting. The space we leave for an answer. The way we listen without already preparing the next question. The willingness to let the encounter begin before deciding where it needs to go.

This is not customer service draped in clinical language.

It is part of the therapeutic alliance.

Technique matters. Assessment matters. Clinical reasoning matters. But each enters a relationship that has already begun forming.

The work before the work is not another technique to master.

It is preparation for everything that follows.

The work begins before touch.

Not with pressure.

With preparation.

Before a practitioner chooses a technique, applies pressure, or explains a treatment plan, another decision has already been made.

It is quieter than the intervention that follows, but often more influential.

The practitioner has decided what they believe is happening.

That belief may be thoughtful and well supported. It may also be shaped by habit, expectation, training, or the understandable desire to solve the problem quickly.

Either way, it becomes the lens through which everything else is interpreted.

We Do Not Assess Without a Lens

Clinical assessment is often presented as if it were a neutral act: observe, palpate, test, interpret, treat.

But we do not enter an assessment empty-handed. We bring our education, previous successes, preferred methods, assumptions, and expectations with us.

These filters help us organize information. They allow experienced practitioners to recognize patterns efficiently.

They can also narrow what we are able to see.

When we become convinced too early that we understand the problem, we may stop listening for information that challenges our first impression. We begin gathering evidence to support a conclusion rather than remaining open to what the client is showing us.

The assessment may continue, but discovery has already ended.

Information Is Not Yet Understanding

A client can provide a great deal of information: where it hurts, when it started, what aggravates it, and what has already been tried.

Our hands provide more: temperature, tone, movement, resistance, guarding, and response.

But information alone does not tell us what it means.

The same muscular tension might reflect load, compensation, apprehension, fatigue, unfamiliarity, or protection. The same limitation in movement may mean something different depending on the person, the environment, and the level of trust present during the assessment.

Clinical understanding develops when we place information in context.

That requires more than collecting findings. It requires listening closely enough to notice how those findings relate to the person in front of us.

The Nervous System Participates in the Examination

Assessment is not something we simply perform on a passive body.

The client is responding to us while we assess them.

Our pace, language, confidence, touch, and expectations all influence what becomes available. A person who feels hurried, judged, or uncertain may present differently from someone who feels heard and included.

Guarding can increase. Movement can become less natural. The client may offer the answer they believe we want instead of the experience they are actually having.

This does not make the assessment unreliable. It makes the relationship part of the assessment.

The state of the nervous system is not interference with the clinical picture. It is part of the clinical picture.

Curiosity Protects Clinical Reasoning

Expertise is not the absence of uncertainty.

It is the ability to remain curious long enough for understanding to develop.

Curiosity allows us to form a hypothesis without becoming trapped by it. It gives the client room to correct us. It helps us notice when their response does not match our expectation.

Instead of asking only, “What technique does this finding indicate?” we can ask:

“What else might explain what I am noticing?”

“What changes when the client feels more supported?”

“What am I assuming—and have I verified it?”

These questions do not weaken clinical confidence. They make it more trustworthy.

Better Decisions Begin With Better Understanding

Technique matters. Precision matters. Experience matters.

But each becomes more useful when guided by an understanding that has not been rushed.

The decision before the decision is the meaning we give to what we see, hear, and feel.

If that meaning is incomplete, even an expertly delivered intervention may address the wrong problem.

Pause before deciding what the client needs.

Listen beyond the first answer.

Let the person—not only the pattern—shape what comes next.

Clinical understanding changes clinical decisions.

The Tao of Clinical Touch explores how safety, attention, permission, and the therapeutic alliance influence everything that follows—including the quality of our clinical decisions.

Available now on Amazon.

The Tao of Listening

A client begins telling us what hurts.

Before they finish, we may already be organizing the information.

We hear “shoulder pain,” and our mind moves toward the shoulder. We hear “sciatica,” and we begin thinking about the hip, the lumbar spine, or the deep rotators. We hear the name of a diagnosis and reach for the techniques, assessments, and patterns we associate with it.

That response is understandable. Clinical experience teaches us to recognize patterns. Education gives us useful categories. Repetition helps us become more efficient.

But efficiency can become anticipation.

And anticipation can quietly replace listening.

The symptom may be the reason the client scheduled the appointment, but it is rarely the entire story. It is often only the first sentence.

Listening Is a Clinical Intervention

Listening is sometimes treated as the polite beginning of the session. We greet the client, collect the necessary information, and then move toward what we consider the real work.

But listening is part of the real work.

How we receive a client’s story may influence what they are willing to tell us. It may affect how accurately we understand the problem. It can reveal what the client fears, what they expect, what they have already tried, and what they believe needs to happen next.

Those details matter.

A client who says, “My neck is always tight,” may be describing discomfort. They may also be describing frustration, interrupted sleep, fear of movement, or the pressure of a problem that no one has taken time to understand.

If we respond too quickly, we may hear the location without understanding the experience.

Clinical listening asks us to remain curious long enough for the fuller picture to emerge.

Not passive.

Not vague.

Not endlessly conversational.

Present, observant, and willing to let the information change what we thought we were going to do.

The Urge to Explain

Practitioners often want to be helpful immediately.

We want the client to know that we recognize the pattern. We want to reassure them that their symptoms make sense. We want to demonstrate that we have a plan.

So we begin explaining.

Sometimes that explanation is useful. Sometimes it is accurate. Sometimes it helps the client feel less uncertain.

But the timing matters.

An explanation offered before the client feels heard may create distance, even when the information is correct. It may tell the client that we have already reached a conclusion. It can shift the session from discovery to confirmation, where every new detail is interpreted through an answer we formed too early.

The question is not whether we should explain.

The question is whether we have listened enough for the explanation to belong to this client.

“Did I Get That Right?”

One of the simplest clinical tools available to us is also one of the most powerful:

“Did I get that right?”

That question does more than confirm facts.

It allows the client to correct us.

It reveals whether we have understood their priority or merely identified their symptoms. It slows the practitioner’s momentum just enough to make room for information that may not fit the first pattern we recognized.

A client may say:

“Yes, but the pain itself is not what worries me. I’m afraid I won’t be able to work.”

Or:

“Mostly, but it only happens after I’ve been sitting.”

Or:

“No. It does not feel tight. It feels like I cannot trust the leg.”

Each clarification can alter the clinical picture.

The client is not simply giving us more words. They are helping us understand what the experience means to them.

When Listening Changes the Plan

Listening becomes clinical when it shapes what happens next.

Perhaps the client’s concern suggests that today should begin with less provocation and more observation.

Perhaps their history tells us that direct work in the painful area has repeatedly increased guarding.

Perhaps their language reveals that predictability is important, so we explain what we are about to do before making contact.

Perhaps what we hear leads us to assess something we might otherwise have overlooked.

Or perhaps the conversation identifies a concern that falls outside our scope and should be referred to another healthcare professional.

Listening does not replace assessment.

It improves the questions we bring to it.

It does not replace technique.

It helps us decide which technique, if any, belongs in this session.

It does not weaken clinical precision.

It gives precision somewhere meaningful to land.

The Information Beneath the Information

Experienced practitioners often develop an ability to notice what is not being said directly.

A change in pace.

A hesitation.

A description that shifts when we ask about a particular movement.

A client who repeatedly says they are “fine” while describing an experience that does not sound fine.

These observations are not diagnoses. They are not invitations to invent meaning or move beyond our scope.

They are reasons to remain curious.

We can ask another question.

We can reflect back what we heard.

We can avoid rushing to fill the silence.

We can allow the client to decide whether there is more they want us to understand.

The goal is not to extract information.

The goal is to create enough room for relevant information to become available.

Listening Before Touch

By the time we place our hands on the client, the therapeutic relationship has already begun.

The client has experienced how we greeted them, whether we interrupted them, how we responded to uncertainty, and whether their priorities influenced the plan.

Touch does not occur separately from that experience.

The first contact carries everything that came before it.

When our listening has been careful, our touch is more likely to arrive with context. We understand where the client is asking for help, what they are prepared for, and what they need from us before we proceed.

That understanding may not produce a dramatic change in technique.

Sometimes it changes something more fundamental.

Timing.

Pressure.

Pacing.

Language.

The decision to proceed.

The decision to wait.

Let What You Heard Change What You Do Next

Listening is not simply being quiet while waiting for our turn to speak.

It is the willingness to be changed by what we hear.

If the client’s answer cannot alter our plan, we may not be asking a clinical question. We may only be collecting confirmation.

The discipline is not to abandon what we know.

It is to hold what we know lightly enough to recognize when this person requires something different.

Before explaining, listen.

Before deciding, clarify.

Before touching, make certain the plan reflects the person in front of you.

The symptom may be the first sentence.

Our responsibility is to listen long enough to understand where the story is asking us to go.

A Clinical Self-Audit

Before your next session, consider:

  • How quickly do I begin forming an explanation?
  • Do my questions invite discovery or confirm my first impression?
  • When did something a client said last change my treatment plan?
  • Do I regularly ask, “Did I get that right?”
  • What might become visible if I listen for one more moment before responding?

Listening becomes clinical when it changes what we do next.

What Are You Actually Assessing?

You have listened to the patient’s history. You have observed their natural movement. You are about to perform your first formal test.

But before you do, pause and ask: What information will this test actually provide in these conditions?

Assessment is not a neutral process. The clinician is part of the assessment field.

Your presence may shape what becomes observable. Your pace may influence how the patient responds. Your language, touch, and expectations all enter the clinical moment before any formal testing begins.

This does not invalidate assessment. It means every finding must be interpreted within the context in which it appeared.

The Clinician Is Part of What You Observe

When you step into the treatment room, you are not an invisible observer. You are part of the environment to which the patient is responding.

Consider a simple example: passive range-of-motion testing.

You perform a passive range test on the patient’s shoulder. End feel is restricted. Guarding is present. You interpret this as mechanical limitation.

But what if the guarding reflects your pace? What if it reflects uncertainty about being moved through an unfamiliar pattern? What if it reflects the subtle pressure in your hands, or the unspoken expectation in the room?

You have encountered restriction and guarding under these particular conditions. Those findings may reflect several influences, including the patient’s current presentation and their response to the testing environment.

These influences are not always cleanly separable. The clinician’s role is to consider how both may be contributing before assigning meaning to the finding.

A patient’s current presentation under relatively settled conditions may differ from their response to urgency, expectation, unfamiliar touch, or perceived pressure.

State and reaction are not always cleanly separable. The distinction is a clinical consideration, not a definitive classification.

The assessment may contain elements of both state and reaction. The distinction is a clinical consideration, not a definitive classification.

History as Context, Not Conclusion

History is the first place this distinction matters.

You ask about mechanism of injury, duration, aggravating and relieving factors, stress, sleep, and occupational demands. The patient tells you their story.

What you are gathering is context for the patient’s symptoms, concerns, and protective behavior.

But if you interrupt, correct their language, or translate their story into a diagnosis before you have observed their movement, early assumptions can narrow what you notice and how you interpret subsequent findings.

History prepares the ground. It does not deliver the conclusion.

Listen without steering. The patient’s narrative helps you understand how they view their situation. If impatience enters the exchange, recognize that it belongs to the clinician, not the patient.

Observation Begins Before Testing

Watch how the patient rises from a chair. How they remove a jacket. Shift weight. Initiate gait. Breathe through movement.

This is genuine assessment. Important information lives here.

Observation may be most informative before the clinician begins directing or correcting movement.

The moment you cue, correct, or demonstrate, the behavior may change. You are no longer observing only the patient’s spontaneous movement strategy. You are also gathering information about how the patient responds to your direction.

This does not make correction wrong. It means timing matters.

Let the body show you how it organizes before you attempt to reorganize it.

Touch as Inquiry

Palpation is not merely pressure. It is inquiry.

The hand applies only enough pressure to encounter a response. Touch contributes information about qualities encountered during palpation, including tenderness, resistance, and guarding.

Guarding may accompany pain, uncertainty, anticipation, or other influences. Pressing through it may alter the response and make the finding harder to interpret.

Instead, maintain contact without deepening pressure. Wait for two full breath cycles.

If tone softens without increased force, this may suggest that protection contributes to the response. It does not rule out structural, neurological, or other influences. Any change observed requires interpretation alongside history, visible movement patterns, and formal testing.

This practical pause contributes to your understanding but does not independently establish whether a limitation is protective, structural, or neurological.

Your patience, restraint, and willingness to wait may influence what becomes available to palpation.

Movement and Testing

When you assess active range of motion, you gather information about how the patient moves under those conditions.

When you perform passive range of motion, you gather information that must be considered alongside symptoms, guarding, history, active movement, and other examination findings.

These are different observations. They require different conditions.

A test performed while the patient is guarding may produce a different finding than the same test performed under different conditions. Neither result should be interpreted apart from the broader clinical picture.

Special orthopedic tests contribute information about symptom reproduction and clinical patterns. They must be interpreted with the broader examination context.

History provides context. Observation contributes information about movement. Touch contributes information about tenderness, resistance, and guarding encountered during palpation. Movement tests may help the clinician consider movement control. Special tests may help clarify symptom reproduction and clinical patterns.

Together, they offer coherence. Individually, they offer incomplete information.

The Difference Between State and Reaction

Rushed assessment may increase guarding or alter how the patient responds.

The patient may guard more in response to speed or pressure. In that case, the finding includes information about the conditions of the assessment.

When you assess patiently and without rushing, observing before directing, listening before interpreting, and waiting before pressing, you may have a better chance of understanding the patient’s current presentation under relatively settled conditions.

Considering this distinction may clarify what you think you know.

If you treat a finding gathered under rushed conditions as context-free, you may overlook the influence of pace or pressure. Even under calmer conditions, findings remain context-dependent and must be considered alongside the rest of the examination.

That consideration can support greater clinical clarity.

Coherence Over Certainty

Assessment does not seek absolute certainty. It seeks coherence: a clearer understanding of how the patient is currently presenting.

Your goal is not to label what is wrong. It is to understand the patient’s current presentation and what conditions might support safer, more sustainable change.

Clearer observation supports more responsible treatment decisions.

Before you interpret, make sure you have perceived clearly.

Before you correct, make sure you have observed genuinely.

Before you press, make sure you have listened.

Careful assessment requires a willingness to recognize that your presence, pace, and expectations may influence what becomes observable.

Awareness of what you are actually assessing, including what the conditions you have created permit you to observe, supports more careful clinical reasoning.

This idea is explored more fully in The Tao of Clinical Touch, which examines how presence, permission, assessment, and restraint shape the clinical encounter.

title.rendered: The Greet Is the First Clinical Intervention

content.rendered:
Your patient walks in. They’re still carrying the momentum of their day—the tension, the pace, whatever happened before they arrived at your door.

These first moments are often treated as a transition into the session. We greet the patient, bring them into the treatment space, and begin gathering information.

But consider a different possibility: the clinical work has already started. Not when you touch them. When they arrive.

The Greet as Clinical Act

The traditional view treats greeting as courtesy before work—small talk that precedes the real business. A warm-up. A social transition.

But something more may happen during those first moments. The patient’s nervous system is actively gathering information. About your pace. Your presence. Whether you seem focused on them or distracted. Whether this session has a shape to it or unfolds unpredictably.

The greet isn’t wasting time before clinical work. It can function as clinical work itself, an opportunity to observe how someone arrives, to orient them to what’s coming, and to establish whether this moment feels manageable and predictable to them.

Consider: a patient who feels oriented, heard, and clear about what comes next may report different information during assessment than one who remains uncertain about the process. Not because one patient is truthful and another isn’t. Because how someone shows up clinically may be influenced by how certain they feel about what’s happening to them.

You Are Part of the Clinical Picture

The clinician is not separate from the clinical environment. Your state, your presence, your pace—these may influence what the patient’s nervous system encounters when they enter your space.

Your pace can influence their pacing. Your presence registers before you speak. Whether you seem fully engaged with this specific person, or partially oriented toward your schedule, or moving quickly between tasks—these cues are available to them.

This touches on what neuroscience calls co-regulation: the nervous system of one person may influence the state of another’s nervous system. It doesn’t mean one person’s state determines another’s outcome. But it may contribute to conditions where regulation becomes more accessible or where vigilance persists.

If you arrive regulated and present, that state exists in the room. If you’re still moving at the pace of your last appointment, or holding the stress of your morning, that lives in the space too. The patient doesn’t need to understand cognitively what’s happening. Their response may be influenced by it, even if they never consciously identify the source.

What a Guarded System Reports

Most clinicians have been trained to gather information quickly: get the history, document the limitations, move to assessment.

Guarding provides meaningful information about how the patient is responding in that moment. It may also obscure aspects of baseline movement or capacity that become clearer as uncertainty decreases.

When a patient arrives tense and uncertain, they may guard tissues, report heightened limitations, restrict motion. This is clinically useful information. It tells you their current protective state. It tells you what they’re expressing through protection. But it may not represent the full picture of what’s accessible to them when they feel more certain about safety.

A greet that helps someone transition from uncertainty toward clarity may create conditions where different information becomes available during assessment. This doesn’t mean the patient was being dishonest before. It means that what someone can show you often depends, in part, on how safe they feel. A protected system shows you protection. A less guarded system may show you something different.

Predictability and Orientation

When a patient doesn’t know what comes next, their attention may organize around anticipating threat. Silence about what you’re going to do. Unexplained transitions between types of touch. A clinician who clearly knows what’s happening but isn’t sharing that information.

All of these may sustain uncertainty.

When a patient knows what to expect—how long this will take, what will happen first, how they should position themselves—some of that uncertainty may ease. They have a frame. They can prepare. They’re not in constant anticipation.

This clarity may help the clinician distinguish between findings that persist and responses influenced by uncertainty about what will happen next.

How You Listen Matters

There are different ways to listen. One way is purposeful and efficient: you ask specific questions designed to confirm or rule out hypotheses. You steer toward what matters for your working clinical picture. You listen for what supports your working assessment.

Another way is broader and less directed: you listen without steering them toward your conclusion. You notice what they bring without immediately pushing it toward the medical model or diagnostic category.

The listening that may support a patient feeling safe is the kind where they experience being genuinely heard rather than interrogated. When the interaction feels interrogative or overly directed, it may influence how the patient responds. Listening without prematurely steering the account can preserve information that might otherwise be missed.

During the greet, this distinction matters.

The Self-Audit

Before your next patient, notice:

When they arrived, what pace were you moving at? Were you fully oriented to them, or was some of your attention still on your schedule or your previous appointment?

Did you explain what the session would include, or move quickly into evaluation? Did you listen to what they brought, or listen primarily for specific diagnostic information?

These aren’t right-or-wrong questions. They’re observations about what actually happened in that first encounter.

If you were moving quickly and thinking about your next patient, they experienced that. If you were calm and fully present, they experienced that too. What matters is noticing what was actually there, not judging it.

Closing

The clinical session doesn’t begin when you place your hands. It begins when the patient arrives. What happens in those first moments may create conditions for what becomes possible during everything that follows.

The greet is not the time before clinical work. It’s a moment where clinical work can begin.

Interested in exploring this framework more deeply?

The Tao of Clinical Touch: The Neuroscience of Permission explores these ideas more fully, including therapeutic alliance, nervous-system regulation, and the clinical decisions that influence how care is experienced.

title.rendered: Presence Before Precision: Your Most Important Clinical Tool Isn’t Your Hands

content.rendered:
You walk into your treatment room for the third patient of the morning. You’ve been rushing between appointments. Your own nervous system is elevated—slightly reactive, moving fast, trying to catch up.

You know your technique is solid. You’ve got good hands. You understand tissue.

But something feels different this morning. Your patient seems guarded. They’re holding more tension than usual. Progress is slower. The same technique that worked brilliantly yesterday isn’t landing today.

The variable isn’t your technique.

It’s your state.

Technique Is Filtered Through Your Regulation

Here’s what most therapists miss: your patient doesn’t experience your technique in a vacuum.

They experience it through the state of your nervous system.

If you’re regulated—grounded, present, and attentive—your technique lands differently than if you’re dysregulated—rushed, distracted, and reactive.

A dysregulated clinician applying perfect technique is still a dysregulated presence in the room. The patient’s nervous system registers this. It can’t fully relax into the work because it’s managing your dysregulation in addition to its own.

A regulated clinician applying average technique is a calm, present, safe presence. The patient’s nervous system can settle into the work.

None of this diminishes the importance of technical skill. It recognizes that technical skill is always expressed through the clinician’s physiological state.

Most clinicians think technique and presence are separate variables.

They’re not.

Presence is the container.

Technique happens inside it.

Presence Isn’t Personality: It’s Preparation

Many clinicians think presence is something you are—a personality trait. Natural warmth. Charisma. Empathy.

It’s not.

Presence is something you prepare for.

The clinician who sits quietly for three minutes before the patient arrives—breathing, grounding, and allowing their nervous system to settle—walks into the room with a different quality than the clinician who rushes from the previous appointment.

Presence is the result of deliberate preparation, not innate personality.

This changes everything.
